nesto: What is a purchase plus improvements mortgage?

blocks.x: Buying a fixer-upper in Winnipeg can be a realistic way into a good neighbourhood. The Winnipeg Regional Real Estate Board reports a record year-to-date detached average of $467,687 across its market region, as of September 2026. A purchase plus improvements mortgage is one way for Winnipeg buyers to pay for the house and the renovation at the same time.
Here's how buyers finance renovations at purchase, and how to plan the project around your budget.
Option 1: Purchase plus improvements mortgage

Many Canadian lenders offer a **purchase plus improvements** mortgage. It adds the cost of planned renovations to your mortgage, so you finance both with one loan. CMHC's insured version is called CMHC Improvement.
**How it typically works:**
You get a detailed contractor quote for the work before you buy.
The lender approves a mortgage based on the home's value **after** the improvements.
At closing, the lender usually holds back the renovation funds. Ask your lender how that works.
The work is completed within the time your lender sets.

The lender confirms the work is done, sometimes with an inspection, then releases the funds to pay the contractor. Because that can come after the work, ask how the contractor gets paid in the meantime, and whether you'll need savings to carry the job until then.
**Good to know:** lenders and mortgage insurers set their own limits and eligible work, so ask your mortgage broker what applies to you.

[CMHC's 2025 fact sheet](https://assets.cmhc-schl.gc.ca/sf/project/cmhc/pdfs/factsheets/new/cmhc-improvement-fact-sheet.pdf) for its insured product, CMHC Improvement, lists up to 95% loan-to-value for owner-occupied homes with one or two units, 90% for three or four units, and 80% for non-owner-occupied rentals of two to four units. Improvement costs of 10% or less of the as-improved value use a single advance, and higher costs use progress advances.
CMHC says additional conditions may apply and this information can change, so confirm the terms with your lender before you rely on them.
Option 2: Refinance or line of credit later

If you buy now and renovate later, you may be able to refinance or use a [home equity line of credit](/blog/home-renovation-financing-canada) once you've built equity. This suits projects that can wait.
Option 3: Government programs and rebates
Check for rebates before you renovate. Energy upgrades like insulation and windows may qualify for Efficiency Manitoba programs. Rules change, so confirm before work starts.
How to plan renovations on a Winnipeg fixer-upper
**Get the quote before you remove conditions.** Your offer should be conditional on financing and inspection. Use that time to have a contractor walk through and price the work.
**Separate must-do from nice-to-have:**

head: Priority
Examples
rows: Foundation cracks, roof, electrical, plumbing, furnace, water in the basement
Kitchen redesign, basement development, layout changes

blocks.x: **Watch for Winnipeg-specific issues.** Older homes on clay soil can show [foundation movement](/blog/clay-soil-basement-cracks-winnipeg). Character homes may have knob-and-tube wiring, or asbestos-containing materials that need testing before demolition.

**Check permits.** Structural changes, basement developments, plumbing and electrical work typically need [City of Winnipeg permits](/blog/winnipeg-renovation-permits). Your lender may ask for proof the work was permitted.
**Build in a contingency** for surprises, especially in older homes.
The bottom line

A fixer-upper can get you into the right home at the right price, if you know the renovation cost before you commit. Get the contractor quote early, talk to your mortgage broker, and plan the must-dos first.
